1.text:
"Alif-Lãm-Mĩm" The chapter opens with three letters of the Arabic alphabet, and the Jalālayn reads them as letters whose meaning God knows best. The Maʿārif commentary explains that this is the first section of the Surah Āl ʿImrān, the third surah of the Qurʾān, and it connects the opening to the prayer that was made at the end of al-Fātiḥah. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the letters as the sign that the Qurʾān is made of the same letters that the Arabs use, and that they were unable to bring one like it. The Mukhtaṣar explains the same point, that the inability of the Arabs to produce a Qurʾān like this is the sign of its divine origin. The Tanwīr reads the letters as a mark of the miracle that the Qurʾān carries. The Qushayrī commentary reads the letters as an allusion to the sufficiency of God for His servant. The Tazkirul commentary states that man has always put many different constructions upon the teachings of God, and that the Qurʾān is a genuine book of guidance. The reader is asked to see the opening letters as a call to the heart before the reading begins, and to see the Qurʾān as the book of guidance that stands above all the constructions that men have placed upon it.

**The letters that open the chapter.**

Alif Lām Mīm God knows best what He means by these letters. This is the first section of Surah 'A1- Imran, the third Surah of the Holy Qur'an.

**A prayer at the end of the first surah.**

It will be recalled that at the end of the Surah Al-Fatihah a prayer for guidance to the straight path was made. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)

**The sign of its origin.**

(Alif. Lam. Mim.) that he said: 'Allah informed us about the story of the delegation of Najran; it is also said that this is an oath by which Allah swore that He is One and that He has neither progeny nor partner. They indicate the inability of the Arabs to bring a Qur’ān like this one despite the fact that it is composed of letters similar to the ones at the beginning of this Sūrah, which also form the parts of their own speech.

**Guidance above constructions.**

But man has always put different constructions upon divine teachings. You are captive to heedlessness and have not found the way to right action and thinking.

**What else the same passage holds.**

After that, by be-ginning the Surah Al-Baqarah with 1 ‌ (This Book which has no doubt in it), it was pointed out that the prayer made in Su-rah Al-Fatihah for guidance to the straight path has been accepted and Allah Almighty has sent down this Qur'an which provides guidance to the straight path. Then came many injunctions of the Islamic law taken up briefly or in details. As a corollary to this, frequent mention was made of the hostility of the disbelievers and the need to confront them. Towards the end, this sequence was concluded with (Help us, then, against disbelieving people) - in the mode of prayer. Since the prayer was made in order that Muslims could confront and prevail over the disbelievers, it was in consonance with that prayer that, in the following Surah 'Al- Imran, the text deals with the modalities of dealing with disbelievers, as well as, with the need to carry out Jihad against them, verbally and physically. This is, so to speak, an elaboration and extension of ‌ ‌ (Help us, then, against disbelieving people).

2.text:
"Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining" The verse opens with the name of Allah and with the declaration that there is no god but Him. The Jalālayn reads the verse as the statement that there is no god except Him, the Living, the Eternal. The Maʿārif commentary takes the words there is no god but He as the central statement of the oneness of God, and it treats the absolute denial of any other god as its full meaning. The Ibn Kathīr commentary reads the Ever-Living as the one who does not die, and the All-Sustaining as the one who maintains all things. The Mukhtaṣar explains that Allah alone deserves to be worshipped, and that He is the one who lives perfectly without any death or deficiency. The Tanwīr reads the Alive as the one who dies not, and the Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the statement that God is not too busy to attend to His servants. The reader is asked to see the verse as the foundation on which the rest of the chapter stands, since every argument that follows rests on this declaration of the oneness and the life of Allah.

**The oneness of Allah.**

In the words (Allah: there is no god but He) which follow immediately, the doctrine of the Oneness of Allah has been put forth as a categorical declaration.

**Worthy of worship.**

It means that there is absolutely nothing worthy of worship other than Allah. (Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists) and,.

**Living and Eternal.**

(Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive) Who dies not and is not evanescent, (the Eternal) the Self-subsistent Who has no beginning. Allah is the One Who alone deserves to be worshipped.

**Maintaining all things.**

But man has always put different constructions upon divine teachings.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The first verse of this section presents a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah; the second verse, the reported proof 1, followed by an answer to some doubts nursed by disbelievers towards the later part. There is no god except Him the Living the Eternal. In the terminology of Islamic theology, a proof based on rational argument is called rational proof while a proof based on a verse of divine book or on a declaration made by an authority or a report narrated by a trustworthy person is called a reported proof. The first word, Alif Lam Mim at the head of the first verse be-longs to the special set of words used by the Qur'an which are words of hidden meaning and are known as Mutashabihat the real meaning of which is a secret between Allah and His Messenger and the details of which appear a little later in the section. Then come the words (the Alive, the All-Sustaining) which lay out a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah. The essence of the argument is that worship means to present oneself before somebody in utter submission and humility. It, therefore, requires that the one who is being worshipped must occupy the highest point of honour and power and who has to be most perfect from all angles. From this it is obvious that anything which cannot sustain its own being, rather is dependent upon somebody else for its very existence, could hardly claim to have any honour or power in its own right.

The Ibn Kathīr commentary reads this as the account of the revelation of Sūrah Āl ʿImrān in al-Madīnah, and it gives the sense that the Book was sent down with truth. The Tanwīr reads the sentence as the statement that Gabriel brought the Scripture to the Prophet. The Mukhtaṣar explains that the Prophet did not know the stories of the earlier peoples, and that Allah revealed them to him. The Qushayrī commentary reads the sending of the Book as a matter of pre-eternal choosing, which came upon the Prophet suddenly. Briefly stated, it means that the principle of tauhid as de-scribed in the Holy Qur'an is not something peculiar to the Qur'an or the Prophet of Islam.

5.text:
"Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah" The verse states that nothing at all is hidden from Allah, whether it is in the earth or in the heaven. The Jalālayn reads the nothing as every existent thing, and it explains that the earth and heaven are named because the senses do not reach beyond them. The Maʿārif commentary takes the verse as the reason why the Creator alone can be the one who is worshipped. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the same sense, that nothing in the earth or in the heaven is hidden from Allah, and that He is the Almighty and the All-Wise. The Tazkirul commentary states that only God can truly tell us what He is in His being and in His attributes, and that the Book makes this clear for the one who seeks. The Mukhtaṣar explains that He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. The Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the statement that a servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it. The reader is asked to see the verse as a sign that the knowledge of Allah reaches to the inner state of every heart, which is the ground for the proofs that follow.

**Nothing is hidden.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. Briefly stated, it means that the principle of tauhid as de-scribed in the Holy Qur'an is not something peculiar to the Qur'an or the Prophet of Islam.

**Only God tells us what He is.**

None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Almighty, the All-Wise. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes.

**Earth and heavens.**

He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden.

**A breath counted.**

A servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it muḥṣīhi. Truly, nothing is hidden from Allah, in the earth or in the heaven He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 3 which follows carries the reported proof of the Oneness of Allah. God specifies them heaven and earth because sensory perception does not go beyond these. On the contrary, Allah Almighty has sent Scrip-tures such as the Torah and the Injil, and His prophets, in earlier times. And this was they all professed and this was they all brought as the message. When the Qur'an came, it simply confirmed their truth. It did not present any new claim which could pose problems for people in its understanding or acceptance. The last two verses further fortify the doctrine of tauhid on the ground that the attributes of encompassing knowledge and unlimited power are strong proofs of His being the One who possesses the eternal, and all-encompassing knowledge and whose power controls every-thing, and that He is the only One who rightly deserves to be wor-shipped. Anyone having imperfect knowledge and limited power can-not be entrusted with this exalted station. Whenever the Holy Qur'an speaks of the 'Torah and the Injil' it refers to the original books revealed to the prophets Moses and Jesus .

6.text:
"He is the One Who shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Almighty, All-Wise" The verse turns to the creation of human beings in the wombs of their mothers. The Jalālayn reads the shaping as the forming of the child as male or female, as Allah wills. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the shaping in the womb is an act of the Creator, which proves that He alone has the power to form the child. The Tanwīr reads the verb as the creating of the child in the wombs, as pleases Him. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the sense that none has the right to be worshipped except Him, the Almighty and the All-Wise. The Tanwīr reads this as the statement that there is no fashioner or creator except Allah. The Mukhtaṣar explains that no one is worthy of being worshipped with love and reverence besides Him. The Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the affirmation of the form of the Creator in the work of creation, which is the sign of His power. The reader is asked to see the verse as the close of the argument from creation, in which the one who forms the child in the womb is the one who alone deserves to be worshipped.

**Shaped in the wombs.**

He it is Who forms you in the wombs as He will as males or females white black or otherwise. Briefly stated, it means that the principle of tauhid as de-scribed in the Holy Qur'an is not something peculiar to the Qur'an or the Prophet of Islam.

**As He wills.**

None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Almighty, the All-Wise. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes.

**No fashioner but Him.**

(There is no God) there is no fashioner or creator (save Him, the Almighty) Who is vengeful against whoever does not believe in Him, (the Wise) in creating what is in wombs. He is the One Who creates you in different forms in the wombs of your mothers, as He wills: as male and female, handsome and ugly, black and white.

**Almighty and All-Wise.**

Talk of this has two sides: the affirmation of the form of the Creator, and the explication of His power over creatures and favor toward them through predetermination and form-giving. (He it is Who fashioneth you) creates you (in the wombs as pleaseth Him) short or tall, pretty or ugly, male or female, felicitous or damned.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 3 which follows carries the reported proof of the Oneness of Allah. Truly, nothing is hidden from Allah, in the earth or in the heaven He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills. There is no god except Him the Mighty in His Kingdom the Wise in His actions. On the contrary, Allah Almighty has sent Scrip-tures such as the Torah and the Injil, and His prophets, in earlier times. And this was they all professed and this was they all brought as the message. When the Qur'an came, it simply confirmed their truth. It did not present any new claim which could pose problems for people in its understanding or acceptance. The last two verses further fortify the doctrine of tauhid on the ground that the attributes of encompassing knowledge and unlimited power are strong proofs of His being the One who possesses the eternal, and all-encompassing knowledge and whose power controls every-thing, and that He is the only One who rightly deserves to be wor-shipped. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. Anyone having imperfect knowledge and limited power can-not be entrusted with this exalted station. Whenever the Holy Qur'an speaks of the 'Torah and the Injil' it refers to the original books revealed to the prophets Moses and Jesus . (He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills.) meaning, He creates you in the wombs as He wills, whether male or female, handsome or otherwise, happy or miserable. (La ilaha illa Huwa (none has the right to be worshipped but He), the Almighty, the All-Wise.) meaning, He is the Creator and thus is the only deity worthy of worship, without partners, and His is the perfect might, wisdom and decision.

7.text:
"He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book, of which some verses are precise—they are the foundation of the Book—while others are elusive. Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking ˹to spread˺ doubt through their ˹false˺ interpretations—but none grasps their ˹full˺ meaning except Allah. As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say, “We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord.” But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason" The verse describes the Book in two kinds of verses, the precise and the elusive. The Jalālayn reads the precise verses as the clear verses, which are the foundation of the Book. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the clear verses settle the doubts raised by those who look for confusion. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the sense that the clear verses are the ones whose meaning is plain, and the elusive are those that have more than one meaning. The Tazkirul commentary states that the reader must understand the difference between the two kinds of verse. The Tanwīr reads the allegorical verses as the verses that are vague in meaning to the people who seek their own ends. The Mukhtaṣar explains that the people of deviation follow the unclear verses to create doubt. The Qushayrī commentary reads the people of firm knowledge as the ones who accept the whole Book as coming from the Lord. The reader is asked to see the verse as the distinction between the seekers of doubt and the people of firm knowledge, who receive the whole Book as the word of their Lord. The reader is asked to hold the precise verses as the anchor of the reading, so that the elusive verses are read in their light and not turned against the clear meaning.

**Precise and elusive verses.**

He it is Who revealed to you the Book wherein are verses that are clear lucid in proof forming the Mother Book the original basis for rulings and others allegorical whose meanings are not known such as the opening verses of some sūras. Through this verse, Allah Almighty has put an end to these doubts by saying that such expressions are in the category of Mutashabihat where the outward meaning is not intended; they are, rather, a secret between Allah and His Messenger, the reality of which cannot become manifest to others for whom it is not even appropriate to go about determining the possible meanings of these words.

**Deviant hearts and doubt.**

It also contains other verses that may have more than one meaning and are puzzling for most people.

**The foundation of the Book.**

There are two kinds of subjects dealt with in the Quran, one pertaining to the known human world, like historical events, signs from the universe and commandments for worldly life; the other pertaining to unseen matters which are not comprehensible by man in this life, for instance, God’s attributes, and the states of Heaven and Hell, etc. Ra; it is also said that (others (which are) allegorical) means: other verses that are abrogated and no longer acted upon.

He it is who has sent down upon thee the Book, wherein are firm verses, which are the mother of the Book, and others ambiguous. (And others (which are) allegorical) vague in their meanings to the Jews, like the use of the letters of the alphabet according to their numerical value (hisab al-Jumal) in such instances as Alif.

And those firmly rooted established and capable in knowledge al-rāsikhūna fī’l-‘ilm is the subject the predicate of which is what follows say ‘We believe in it the allegorical part that it is from God and we do not know its meaning; all of the clear and the allegorical is from our Lord’; yet none remembers yadhdhakkar the initial tā’ of yatadhakkar has been assimilated with the dhāl that is none is admonished but people of pith possessors of intellect who when they see those following that allegorical part only also say The Holy Prophet refuted their doctrine of Trinity in details and proved the Oneness of Allah with reference to the eternal existence, the perfect power, the all encompassing knowledge; and the most unique creativity of Allah Almighty who had to be One and indivisible. The Christians had to accept these premises and once tauhid was proved, the converse, that is, the belief in Trinity was also proved untenable. The Christians then expressed their doubts about some words of the Holy Qur'an in which Sayyidna 'Isa i.e. Jesus Christ has been called 'Ruhullah ' (the Spirit of Allah) or 'Kalimatullah ' (the Word of Allah), which according to them led to prove that Sayyidna Isa had a share in the divinity of Allah. One has to have faith in them by believing that whatever Allah Almighty has elected to mean through them is the truth. It is not permissible to dig deeper and mount further researches in this direction. Allah Almighty has, by Mentioning Muhkamat and : Mutashabihat right there in the beginning, pointed out towards a general principle which, if understood, could eradicate many doubts and disputes. The principle is that the Holy Qur'an has two kinds of verses; one is known as the Muhkamat (of established meaning) and the other as the Mutashabihat (whose definite meanings are unknown). Muhkamat is the name of verses the meaning of which is open and clear to one who knows the rules of Arabic grammar fairly well. But when the meanings and explanations of particular verses are not clear to such' a person, then, such verses are called the Mutashabihat . Allah Almighty has called the first kind of verses, that is, the Muhkamat Umm al-Kitab ' (which has been translated literally as 'mother verses') meaning thereby that such verses are the very root and essence of all teachings, and the meanings and explanations of which are free of doubt or ambiguity. Since the exact intention of the second kind of verses, that is, the Mutashabihat remains ambiguous and uncertain, therefore, the correct method of their interpretation would be to harmonize them with the first kind, that is, the Muhkamat . Then, the rule is that any interpretation of the Mutashabihat which goes against the first kind should be rejected absolutely and only that interpretation should be given credence which is not against the verses of established meaning (Muhkamat). For example, the Holy Qur'an has clarified the position of Sayyidna Isa (Jesus Christ) by saying (he is nothing but a servant upon whom We have bestowed Our blessing 43:59), or as elsewhere in the Qur'an, by ‌ (the example of Isa before Allah is like that of Adam whom He created from clay - 3:59). These and several other verses like them show it clearly that Sayyidn Isa Masih, is a chosen servant of Allah created by Him. Therefore, the claim of Christians investing him with godhood and son ship is not correct. Now, if someone closes his eyes towards all these verses which have an established meaning and unnecessarily coils with the expressions, (the Word of Allah) and ‌ (a spirit from Him) and their likes from the category of Mutashabihat (verses whose definite meanings cannot be ascertained) and starts deducing from them meanings which are against the Muhkamat of Qur'an and other consistent statements, then, that would be a simple case of going astray and being ob-stinate.

8.text:
"˹They say,˺ “Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us. Grant us Your mercy. You are indeed the Giver ˹of all bounties˺" The verse gives the prayer of those who are well grounded in knowledge, who ask their Lord to keep their hearts steady after the guidance has come. The Jalālayn reads the prayer as the request that the Lord not cause the hearts to incline toward falsehood. The Maʿārif commentary explains that these people chose to have faith in what comes from their Lord, and that they ask Him to keep them on the path. The Ibn Kathīr commentary reads the mercy as the grace that the believers ask from Allah to keep their hearts firm. The Tanwīr reads the Giver as the one who bestows every good upon the believer, and the Mukhtaṣar explains that Allah is the one who saves from what befell those who moved away from the truth. The Tazkirul commentary states that one should be content with an abstract understanding of the things that are beyond the senses, and that the believer must accept what he cannot fully see. The Qushayrī commentary reads the prayer as a plea for a bounty that is not repaid by any deed, but given by mercy alone. The reader is asked to see the verse as the prayer of the firm in knowledge, who fear the turning of the heart and seek the mercy of their Lord to keep it steady.

**Our hearts do not deviate.**

Our Lord do not cause our hearts to deviate do not cause them to incline away from the truth in their desire to interpret it such as is inappropriate for us — as You caused the hearts of those others to deviate — after You have guided us after You have shown us the way to it; and give us mercy from You as a strengthening; You are the Bestower. Instead of that, they elected to have faith in what comes from their Lord.

**Grant us Your mercy.**

(they follow that which is not entirely clear thereof) meaning, they refer to the Mutashabih, because they are able to alter its meanings to conform with their false interpretation since the wordings of the Mutashabihat encompass such a wide area of meanings. One should be content to have an abstract understanding of the things which cannot be grasped precisely by the senses.

**The Giver of all bounties.**

(Lo! Thou, only Thou art the Bestower) to the believers before us; it is also said that this means: Save us from what happened to those who moved away from the truth.

**Content with what the senses miss.**

And give what you give, O Lord, as Your bounty and mercy, not as the recompense for our works or the compensation for our acts of obedience! (Cause not our hearts to stray) do not make our hearts deviate from Your Religion (after Thou hast guided us) to Your Religion, (and bestow upon us mercy from Thy Presence) make us firm in holding to Your religion.

**What else the same passage holds.**

In it are verses that are entirely clear, they are the foundations of the Book; and others not entirely clear. So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. The previous verse mentioned 'those well-grounded in knowledge' who, in spite of their excellent knowledge, were not proud of their excellence. The present verse mentions yet another excellence of theirs - that they pray for steadfastness on the right path, not for any worldly gains, but for salvation in the life-to-come. The first verse shows us that guidance and straying are from Allah alone. When Allah intends to guide someone, He makes his heart tilt towards what is good and right; and when He decides to let someone go astray, He turns his heart away from the straight path. This is just as it was said in a hadith of the Holy Prophet There is no heart which is not there in between the two of Allah's fingers - He makes it firm on the truth as long as He wills, and turns it away from the truth when He wills. Therefore, those who are concerned about how to remain firm in their faith, they go to the source - requesting and praying Allah for steadfastness. The Holy Prophet always used to pray for it as it appears in a hadith: ( O reverser of hearts, make our hearts firm on the faith chosen by You).

9.text:
"Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day—about which there is no doubt. Surely Allah does not break His promise.”" The verse turns to the Day of Gathering, which the believers ask their Lord to bring about in the proper time. The Jalālayn reads the gathering as the bringing together of mankind for a day that is certain to come. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the first verse of this passage shows that guidance and straying are from Allah, and that the believer asks for the gathering on that Day. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the sense that Allah keeps His promise, and that the Day is sure to come as He has promised. The Tanwīr reads the gathering as the act of Allah, who brings people together after they die. The Tazkirul commentary states that man turns away from the truth in order to safeguard his worldly interests, and that the Day of Gathering is the answer to this. The Qushayrī commentary reads the Day as the gathering of the lovers of God in the presence of their Lord. The reader is asked to see the verse as the close of the prayer of the firm in knowledge, who look to the certain Day as the place where the promise of their Lord is kept. The reader is asked to see the verse as the place where the prayer for the Day is joined to the certainty of the promise, so that the believer waits for the Day with hope and with trust in the word of his Lord.

**The gathering of mankind.**

Our Lord You shall gather mankind for a day that is on a day of which there is no doubt no uncertainty that is the Day of Resurrection when You will requite them for their deeds as You had promised; verily God will not fail the tryst His promise of the Upraising there is a shift of address here from the second to the third person and these last words could constitute God’s speech. The first verse shows us that guidance and straying are from Allah alone.

**The promise is kept.**

So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. Our Lord, You are going to call all people back to You: to hold them to account on a day in which there is no doubt.

**It is Thou who gathers.**

(it is Thou Who gatherest mankind together) after they die (to a Day) on a day (of which there is no doubt. Lo! Allah faileth not to keep the tryst) resurrection after death, the reckoning, the Bridge over hell, the Scale, Paradise and hell. On the one hand, there are all the assets of worldly comfort and grandeur, while, on the other hand, there is the caravan of truth, having no foothold in society, and no worldly interests attached to it.

**The gathering of the lovers.**

Today is the gathering of the lovers on the carpet of approach iqtirāb and tomorrow will be the gathering of all in the place of reward thawāb and punishment ʿiqāb. That is why, in order to safeguard his interests, man turns away from the truth.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The purpose of their supplication in this way is to show that their concern is with the matter of the Hereafter and for this reason they ask God for adherence to the path of guidance in order to attain its reward. In it are verses that are entirely clear, they are the foundations of the Book; and others not entirely clear. The two Shaykhs Bukhārī and Muslim reported that ‘Ā’isha may God be pleased with her said ‘The Messenger of God s recited this verse It is He Who revealed to you the Book wherein are verses clear to the end of the verse and said “When you see those pursuing the allegorical parts know that these are the ones God refers to in this verse so beware of them” ’. Al-Tabarānī reported in his al-Kabīr that Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī heard the Prophet s say ‘I fear nothing for my community except three faults’ and he mentioned that one of these would be when the Book is opened in front of them and the believer will desire to interpret it and yet none knows its interpretation save God; and those firmly rooted in knowledge say ‘We believe in it all is from our Lord; yet none remembers but people of pith’ Q. 37 end of the hadīth. And those who are firmly grounded in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord. " And none receive admonition except men of understanding (They say): Let not our hearts deviate (from the truth) after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from You. Verily, it is You Who will gather mankind together on the Day about which there is no doubt. The previous verse mentioned 'those well-grounded in knowledge' who, in spite of their excellent knowledge, were not proud of their excellence. Instead of that, they elected to have faith in what comes from their Lord. The present verse mentions yet another excellence of theirs - that they pray for steadfastness on the right path, not for any worldly gains, but for salvation in the life-to-come. Allah states that in the Qur'an, there are Ayat that are Muhkamat, entirely clear and plain, and these are the foundations of the Book which are plain for everyone. When Allah intends to guide someone, He makes his heart tilt towards what is good and right; and when He decides to let someone go astray, He turns his heart away from the straight path. This is just as it was said in a hadith of the Holy Prophet There is no heart which is not there in between the two of Allah's fingers - He makes it firm on the truth as long as He wills, and turns it away from the truth when He wills. Therefore, those who are concerned about how to remain firm in their faith, they go to the source - requesting and praying Allah for steadfastness. The Holy Prophet always used to pray for it as it appears in a hadith: ( O reverser of hearts, make our hearts firm on the faith chosen by You).
